newsitem.title: UK: UK MPs urge curbs on out-of-town leisure complexes.
newsitem.headline: UK MPs urge curbs on out-of-town leisure complexes.

text.p: Parliament's Environment Committee urged the government on Wednesday to restrict the development of out-of-town leisure complexes.

The cross-party panel, whose report in 1994 spurred the government to introduce tougher planning guidelines for out-of-town shopping centres, said it was now particularly concerned about the rapid growth of multi-screen cinemas, known as megaplexes.
It said a further 50 of these cinemas, with up to 30 screens each and more than 1,000 parking spaces, could be developed over the coming years.

The committee said in a report it was encouraged that junior environment minister Robert Jones had made clear his intention to take a tough approach to multiplex cinemas and urged him to pass the same message on to local planning authorities.
Urging the Department of Environment to complete speedily a research project it has launched on the question, the MPs said:

"Thereafter ministers should be prepared to act quickly to amend the present guidance with the objective of seeking to restrict the development of large-scale leisure developments outside existing town centres."
The committee's chairman, Andrew Bennett, said he was alarmed at the pace of out-of-town lesiure developments and pleased that all members of the panel backed the call for curbs.

"These represent the latest threat to existing town centres as places where people not only shop but live, work and relax. I am very concerned that where one function of a centre is allowed to die, others may follow," Bennett said in a statement.
The panel's report also called for car parks at out-of-town developments to be taxed, either through a levy or by allowing local authorities to assess car parks for business rates.
Two years after the committee's first report, Bennett said the new sequential approach to out-of-town planning had successfully prevented further damage to most high streets.
He said he was also by and large reassured that the government was managing to protect smaller towns and market towns that supermarket developers are now targeting.

But he said the government could do more, for example by giving more assistance to local authorities seeking to use their compulsory purchase powers to promote alternative retail developments in town centres.
The report also includes calls for grater support for town centre management, more work on retail impact studies and improvement to the operation of the planning system.

"There is nothing particularly radical in this report, because by and large the system is working well and the right policies are in place. I therefore see no reason why the government should not accept our modest proposals in their entirety," Bennett said.
